spec.title: Read the request lifecycle on the wire
spec.intro:
You are handed the real artifacts of one request lifecycle — the moment "example.com" becomes
pixels — and asked to read each control claim's truth directly off them. A name resolved (DNS), a
channel opened and secured (TCP/TLS), an identity proven (the certificate): every stage is a place
a claim can be made or broken, and you will point to the exact message, byte, or field that holds
each one.

This surface composes the real lifecycle. The DNS query and response are PEELable byte-range trees
— select a region and the RFC 1035 parser shows the real decode. The DNS delegation and the TLS 1.3
handshake are orderable sequences run by their real state machines — route the leaf query to the
root and it returns the real referral; play data before the handshake finishes and TLS returns the
real unexpected_message alert. The certificate is the real www.google.com leaf (and a broken twin).
Nothing is invented; the message, the state machine, and the certificate are the answer key. Start
on the DNS query panel.

tasks.instruction:
On the DNS query panel, select QDCOUNT (`dns.qdcount`) and confirm it reads as one question
pending. This is one of the four 16-bit counts in the fixed 12-byte header.

hints.nudge: The header is a fixed 12 bytes; one of its four counts says how many questions are pending.

hints.concept: §4.3 — the header packs an ID, a flags word, then four counts: QDCOUNT/ANCOUNT/NSCOUNT/ARCOUNT

hints.reveal: Select dns.qdcount — it reads 1 (one question pending)

tasks.explain:
QDCOUNT=1 says one question is pending. The header is read entirely off fixed offsets — the ID,
the flags word, and the four counts — every value at the place RFC 1035 §4.1.1 fixed it.

tasks.instruction:
Select the QNAME (`dns.qname`) and decode the length-prefixed labels to the name they spell. A
name is not stored with dots — each chunk is preceded by a length byte and ends at a zero
terminator.

hints.nudge: There are no dots in the wire format; each label is preceded by a one-byte length.

hints.reveal: Select dns.qname — the labels 07 'example' 03 'com' 00 decode to example.com

tasks.explain:
The QNAME `07 'example' 03 'com' 00` decodes to example.com — the name you typed, encoded as the
RFC 1035 §3.1 label sequence. The parser produces the same decode you can do by hand from the
bytes; there is no answer key, only the wire.

tasks.instruction:
Select QTYPE (`dns.qtype`) and report which record type this query asks for. It sits right after
the QNAME's zero terminator.

hints.nudge: The query's last fields follow the QNAME terminator; the type names the record wanted.

hints.concept: §4.3 — QTYPE names the record: A=1, CNAME=5, CAA=257; CLASS IN=1

hints.reveal: Select dns.qtype — it reads 1 = A (the IPv4 address record)

tasks.explain:
QTYPE A means "give me the IPv4 address for this name." The query is fully read — a name and a
record type — each value at its RFC-fixed offset.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the DNS response panel and select ANCOUNT (`dns.ancount`) — read how many answer
records returned for this name.

hints.nudge: The same four header counts appear in the response; one says how many answers came back.

hints.concept: §4.3 — ANCOUNT is the answer count in the header (RFC 1035 §4.1.1)

hints.reveal: Select dns.ancount on the response — it reads 2 (two answers returned)

tasks.explain:
ANCOUNT=2 says two answer records came back. The response is the same structure as the query —
header, question echo, then resource records — and the count tells you how many RRs to peel.

tasks.instruction:
Select the first Answer record's RDATA (`dns.answer.0.rdata`) and read the resolved address — an
A record's RDATA is four bytes decoded to a dotted IPv4 quad.

hints.nudge: Each Answer RR ends in its RDATA; for an A record that is the four-byte address.

hints.concept: §4.3 — an A record's RDATA is four octets decoded to a dotted quad (RFC 1035 §4.1.3)

hints.reveal: Select dns.answer.0.rdata — the first A record reads 104.20.23.154

tasks.explain:
The first RDATA decodes to 104.20.23.154 — the real address the live resolver returned. The
address you now have is exactly what the next stage (TCP) needs; the lifecycle's first handoff is
complete, read entirely off the bytes.

tasks.instruction:
Select the response's flags word (`dns.flags`) and read the AD bit. State whether this answer was
DNSSEC-validated — and name the one thing AD does NOT tell you about the lookup.

hints.nudge: The AD (Authenticated Data) bit lives in the flags word; a validating resolver sets it.

hints.concept: §4.3 — AD=1 means the resolver verified DNSSEC signatures on the DATA (RFC 4035)

hints.reveal: Select dns.flags — AD reads 0: this answer was NOT DNSSEC-validated

tasks.explain:
AD=0 is a real control reading: this answer came back without DNSSEC validation, so the
name-to-address mapping's integrity rests on the resolver and the path, not a signature you can
check (SC-12/SC-17). And note the trap — AD speaks only about the DATA's authenticity; it says
nothing about whether the query travelled encrypted. Those are two different controls at one stage.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the DNS delegation TRACE. Order the messages so the stub asks ONE recursive query and
the recursive resolver walks root → TLD → authoritative iteratively, routing each message between
the right participants. The sim accepts the chain only when it reaches the answer.

hints.nudge: Only ONE participant does all the legwork; the servers above only point one step further.

hints.concept: §4.2 — the stub asks recursively (RD=1); the resolver queries the hierarchy iteratively, and a referral is not an answer

hints.reveal: Order: stub→recursive query, recursive→root, root→recursive referral, recursive→tld, tld→recursive referral, recursive→authoritative, authoritative→recursive answer, recursive→stub answer

tasks.explain:
The recursive resolver does the legwork while root and TLD only refer one step further — a
referral is not an answer. The sim reaching the authoritative answer is the protocol's real
consequence, not a stored "correct"; route the leaf query straight to the root and it returns the
real referral to the .com servers, because a root server refers, it never answers a leaf.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the TLS 1.3 handshake TRACE. Order the message cards into the RFC 8446 full handshake,
routing each onto Client or Server, until the sim reaches its established state — the channel
opens application data only when the order is legal.

hints.nudge: The client speaks first; the server answers and proves itself before anything is encrypted; both sides Finish.

hints.concept: §4.5 — ClientHello → ServerHello → EncryptedExtensions → Certificate → CertificateVerify → server Finished → client Finished

hints.reveal: Order: ClientHello, ServerHello, EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, server Finished, client Finished

tasks.explain:
The order is causal: CertificateVerify (the server signing the transcript) must follow
Certificate (the public key), so the client has something to check the signature against. The sim
reaching the established state is the consequence — the real RFC 8446 §A.1 state machine, not an
authored "correct."

tasks.instruction:
In the same TLS handshake, play application data BEFORE the Finished messages are exchanged (the
classic break). Read the alert the sim raises and its numeric code — the protocol's real refusal,
not a "try again."

hints.nudge: The data channel does not exist until both Finished messages are sent — the sim tells you how it objects.

hints.concept: §4.5 — RFC 8446 §6.2: a message out of the permitted order MUST terminate with unexpected_message(10)

hints.reveal: Inject ApplicationData before the Finished messages; the sim raises unexpected_message(10)

tasks.explain:
unexpected_message(10) is the literal RFC 8446 §6.2 alert the state machine emits — the
handshake's order is structural, not advisory. Confidentiality begins only after both Finished are
exchanged, and the protocol enforces it with a real code you can read, exactly like TCP's RST.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the "Cert · www.google.com leaf" panel and select the Subject Alternative Name
(`cert.san`). Read the host it covers — this is the field that ties the certificate back to the
name that rode, in plaintext, in the TLS ClientHello's SNI.

hints.nudge: A certificate is valid only for the names in one extension — find the host list.

hints.concept: §4.6 — RFC 5280 Subject Alternative Name carries the host(s) the cert covers; it must match the SNI host

hints.reveal: Select cert.san on the leaf; it reads DNS:www.google.com — the host the plaintext SNI named

tasks.explain:
The SAN binds this certificate's key to a name, and that name is the same one that travelled in
the clear in the ClientHello SNI (the metadata the encryption boundary leaves exposed, §4.4). If
the host you connected to is not in the SAN, the channel is encrypted but pointed at the wrong
door — name-to-key binding is what a certificate IS (RFC 5280), and it anchors the identity half
of "encrypted in transit" (SC-23).

tasks.instruction:
Switch to "Cert · wrong.host.badssl.com (broken)". This real certificate breaks the "we are
talking to the real site" claim at exactly one field. Select the single field where it fails to
cover the host you connected to (`cert.san`) and read its value.

hints.nudge: The padlock is valid — but for the wrong name. Read the SAN and compare it to wrong.host.badssl.com.

hints.concept: §4.6 — a SAN that does not cover the connected host is a hostname mismatch (RFC 6125), openssl verify code 62

hints.reveal: On the wrong-host panel, select cert.san — it covers *.badssl.com / badssl.com, NOT wrong.host.badssl.com

tasks.explain:
The SAN reads DNS:*.badssl.com, DNS:badssl.com — a single-label wildcard that does NOT cover the
three-label wrong.host.badssl.com (RFC 6125), so the cert is valid but for the wrong door:
hostname mismatch, openssl verify code 62 (SC-23). The discriminating field is the parser's
computed divergence over the real bytes, not your opinion — your Lifecycle Evidence Finding names
the stage, the field, both values, the broken control, and the framework reference.

tasks.instruction:
In 5–7 sentences, for a non-technical colleague: explain how typing example.com becomes pixels as
a chain of handoffs (name → connection → secure channel → identity → conversation) and why each
handoff is a place a control claim lives; why a DNS referral is not an answer; and why "encrypted
in transit" begins only after the handshake — so the name you looked up and the host in the SNI
travelled in the clear. Use the §3 sealed-letter model, not jargon.

hints.nudge: The §3 model: asking around for an address, a knock-and-answer, a sealed channel, a vouched-for credential.

hints.concept: §3 — The Mental Model + §4.4 the encryption boundary

fields.proves: server holds the private key for the cert's public key
